price_per_million.source: copied from reasoning_models_v1 (confirmed 2026-11-11); thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: opponent next-possession PPP after play type X (aftershock)
own-sequence lag effects (own next possession after X)
play-type labeling quality (foul buckets, initiation_type mapping)
methodological_questions: Is the opponent next-possession PPP shift after X play-type-specific, or generic to any possession ending, so that it would not discriminate between play types?
Is the shift big enough to change an AVOID label, given a pre-specified label rule and threshold?
Do own-sequence lags carry signal beyond the current play type, at the sample sizes available?
How much of any next-possession effect is mechanical (made basket gives an inbound, a miss or turnover gives transition) or comes from labeling artifacts (OTHER/DRIVE foul leakage)?
What multiplicity control is needed across play types and pairs?

historical_evidence.finding: [APPA-049] Opponent-next 'aftershock' replicated for 8/8 play types in all games and playoffs (CUT +0.119, n=21,398, playoffs +0.131, n=1,145; through TRANSITION +0.135, n=26,262, playoffs +0.126, n=1,529). [APPS-037] Aftershock after success is uniformly positive, +0.119 to +0.135 across play types (per-PT n 5.9k-57.6k; opp-next n=458,604). Aftershock is defined as opponent-next baseline 1.206 minus opponent PPP after X succeeds (about 1.07-1.09); positive means the opponent scores less. The own-next baseline is 0.975 PPP (n=18,943), and own-next (A1) was treated as exploratory (~4% of pairs). The record notes that the uniform shift 'may be a generic dead-ball/score effect rather than PT-specific disruption'. It also notes a sign-convention conflict with a 52-series net-swing table, tiny-n team cells marked significant at |t|>=2.0, only same_pipeline_validation, members_disagree=yes, and a LIM:small_sample limitation. APPS-037's verdict is recorded as 'descriptive'.

Labeling audit: OTHER has 36% foul endings and inflated PPP (FOUL_BUCKET). DRIVE sits 12pp below the foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK). PNR shows a 22% foul rate. Only 335 of 50,668 possessions (0.7%) map to a real play type via initiation_type. Verdict: artifact_found.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Reading play-type PPP differences as real efficiency without handling foul-ending leakage, and relying on initiation_type to map possessions to play types
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as C_artifact: OTHER PPP inflated by 36% foul endings, DRIVE 12pp below the foul benchmark, and initiation_type mapping only 0.7%.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using a uniform aftershock against an unmatched opponent-next baseline as evidence of play-type-specific defensive disruption
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as an unresolved concern: the uniformly positive shift across all play types may be a generic dead-ball/score effect. Team-level cells were marked significant at tiny n, and validation used the same pipeline.

evidence_establishes: [FAM:SF07, supported, APPA-049] In the earlier pipeline, opponent PPP on the next possession after X succeeds is lower than the pooled opponent-next baseline by about 0.12-0.135 PPP for all 8 play types, in all games and in playoffs.
[FAM:SF07] The aftershock magnitudes are nearly identical across play types (range about 0.016 PPP), and the own-next effect was only treated as exploratory (~4% of pairs, n=18,943).
[FAM:SF-CHT-025, artifact] Play-type labels in the derived data have recorded foul-ending leakage (OTHER, DRIVE, PNR), and initiation_type mapping was almost entirely non-informative (0.7%).
evidence_does_not_establish: That the opponent-next effect differs between play types enough to change which play types are labeled AVOID. The record shows near-uniformity, which argues against differential labeling.

That the aftershock is causal or play-type-specific rather than a mechanical or generic dead-ball effect (inbound after a make versus transition after a miss), or that the baseline of 1.206 is a matched comparison.
Anything about own-sequence lags beyond an exploratory, small-n descriptive finding.
The AVOID rule or threshold, or whether any label would flip under adjustment. Neither record states this.
Whether the findings hold after the foul-leakage correction, on independent pipelines, or on data not used in SF07 (including 2025-26).
own_inferences: If the aftershock is about +0.12-0.135 for every play type, adding it to a net-value label shifts all play types almost equally. Rank order, and therefore relative AVOID status, would change little unless the threshold is absolute.

The aftershock probably depends on how X ended (make, miss, turnover, foul) and on game state, so it should be modeled as a function of the ending event. The 'success' conditioning in APPS-037 builds this in.

The opponent-next baseline of 1.206 is much higher than the 1.07-1.09 conditional values and the own-next 0.975. This looks like a baseline composition mismatch (for example, including possessions after steals or live-ball turnovers), so the aftershock may be inflated.
Own-sequence tests will be underpowered: about 4% of pairs spread over 8 play types leaves roughly 2k pairs per play type, with a minimum detectable effect of about 0.07 PPP.
Foul leakage into OTHER and DRIVE could bias the play-type-specific contrasts even if the overall aftershock is real.
uncertainties: The definition of the AVOID label and the threshold for 'large enough to drive' is not specified in the task or the records.
Whether the 2025-26 playoffs are in the frozen data: they are partial on 2026-06-19 and complete on 2026-06-21.
How the pooled baseline was built and whether conditioning on X's success was matched on game state.
Whether the SF07 sign convention is applied consistently elsewhere in the project, given the opposite sign in the net-swing table.
The amount of overlap between SF07's sample and any new test (the same pipeline was used for validation).

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I would have treated this as a direct test of a plausible effect. SF07 showed that the aftershock is large and uniform, which shifts the question from 'is there an effect' to 'does it discriminate between play types'. SF07's own notes also flag the generic dead-ball caveat. SF-CHT-025's labeling artifacts and the 0.7% initiation_type mapping led me to require foul-ending handling and outcome-conditioned, play-type-matched baselines. The decision moved from proceed to proceed_with_changes.

blocking_constraints.text: Foul-ending leakage in OTHER/DRIVE/PNR and weak initiation mapping (0.7%) can distort play-type-specific contrasts. Foul endings must be excluded or modeled separately before a labeling claim is made.
Own-sequence (own-next) pairs are ~4% of pairs (n~18.9k total, ~2k per play type), so only large lag effects (~0.07 PPP) are detectable. Claims about own-sequence lags are likely to be exploratory.

prior_work.summary: SF07 documents a uniform opponent-next aftershock (+0.12 to +0.135 PPP) across 8 play types and treats own-next as exploratory. It does not test whether the effect is large enough to change AVOID labels or whether it is play-type-specific. SF-CHT-025 shows labeling artifacts that can contaminate play-type comparisons.

risks.text: Opponent next-possession PPP depends on how X ended (made basket versus miss versus turnover), on game state, on lineup quality, and on the intervening dead-ball. A generic dead-ball/score effect is not play-type disruption.

After a make the next possession is an inbound half-court set. After a miss or turnover it can be transition, which scores more. Play-type success rates differ, so next-possession PPP differs mechanically.
Foul buckets (OTHER 36%, PNR 22%) and DRIVE foul leakage can bias play-type PPP and the next-possession comparisons.
The aftershock is conditioned on X 'succeeding' (an outcome), and AVOID labels may be derived from outcomes, which creates circularity.
If AVOID labels are assigned from past PPP and then evaluated on the same data, regression to the mean and selection will inflate effects.
The baselines (1.206 opponent-next, 0.975 own-next) are not matched to the conditioned samples. The 1.206 value looks high compared with the conditional values.
Own-sequence cells are small (4% of pairs). Team-level and pair-level cells are tiny (n=16-18 cells marked significant at |t|>=2 in SF07).
8 play types x 2 directions plus 64 pairs without correction produce false positives.
SF07 was validated only within the same pipeline. A placebo must show that the same shift appears for non-play-type events.
Four seasons plus playoffs; pace, shot profile and rule/definition changes may shift baselines. The 2025-26 playoffs are partial.
Play-type labels derived from the full play-by-play sequence could use information from after X, such as the next possession's outcome.
Sign-convention inconsistency (aftershock positive means opponent scores less) versus the net-swing table, and any possession-linking errors, can reverse conclusions.

design.estimand: Play-type-specific opponent next-possession PPP effect: for each X, the difference between opponent PPP on the immediately following possession and the PPP after matched possession endings of all other play types, adjusted for X's ending event, score margin, period/clock bucket, team and opponent strength, and home/away. A secondary estimand is the own-next PPP difference for the same contrasts. The label question is: would any play type's AVOID status change if the adjusted next-possession effect were added to its own-possession net value under a pre-specified rule? Pre-register the AVOID rule and a materiality threshold (for example, a play-type-specific effect of at least 0.03 PPP relative to the cross-play-type mean, or a label flip) before running.
design.unit: Consecutive possession pair (X possession, next possession) within a game; clustered by game and team.
design.sample: Frozen snapshot of NBA 2022-23 through 2024-25 regular seasons and playoffs, plus the 2025-26 regular season (complete 2026-04-13). Exclude the 2025-26 playoffs from the primary analysis because they are partial on 2026-06-19; use them as an untouched confirmation set only after they are complete (2026-06-21) and the design is frozen. Exclude end-of-period, garbage-time, and intervening-timeout/injury possessions. Exclude or separately model foul-ending possessions and the OTHER bucket.
design.power: Per-play-type n of 5.9k-57.6k for opponent-next gives SE of about 0.005-0.015 (PPP SD ~1.15), so differences of 0.03 PPP are detectable with 80% power after Holm adjustment for most play types, though less so for PUTBACK. Own-next has ~2k pairs per play type (minimum detectable ~0.07 PPP), so it is exploratory. Report confidence intervals and the minimum detectable effect per cell.
design.controls: Condition on X's ending event (make, miss with offensive or defensive rebound, turnover type, foul), score margin, quarter, clock, home, team and opponent offensive/defensive rating, and rest. Use a mixed model with team, opponent and game random effects. Use a baseline matched on ending event and game state, not the pooled opponent-next baseline of 1.206. Fix one sign convention (positive = opponent scores less) and document it. Use the derived play-type labels only after the foul-leak fix; report a sensitivity analysis excluding DRIVE, PNR and OTHER if the labeling fix is not complete.
design.falsification: (1) Placebo: lag-2 effect (X two possessions earlier), which should be null after conditioning. (2) Permute play-type labels within game and ending-event strata; the apparent play-type differences should vanish. (3) Pre-treatment check: opponent PPP on the possession before X should not depend on X. (4) Generic dead-ball comparison: the same shift for non-play-type possession endings (for example, defensive-rebound or turnover endings) of matched type. (5) Split the data by season to check stability of the effect and rank order, and by regular season versus playoffs. If the effect is uniform across play types (range under the materiality threshold), conclude 'not differential, does not drive AVOID labels'.
design.multiplicity: Primary family: 8 play types x opponent-next effect = 8 tests with Holm correction at alpha=0.05. Own-next (8 tests) is a secondary family with Holm separately. The 64 X->Y pair premiums are exploratory under BH FDR at 10%; no team-level cells with n<100.
design.decision_rule: Supported if at least one play type has an adjusted opponent-next effect differing from the cross-play-type mean by at least the pre-registered threshold (Holm-adjusted p<0.05, CI excluding zero), the AVOID label changes under the pre-registered rule, the effect is stable across seasons, and placebo/permutation checks are null. Rejected if all play-type contrasts have CIs within the threshold and the power is adequate (the uniform aftershock result). Artifact if the effect vanishes after conditioning on ending event or foul handling, or the generic dead-ball comparison reproduces it. Uncertain otherwise. Own-sequence conclusions require the same rule and are reported as exploratory unless the CI width allows a 0.07 effect to be excluded.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API play-by-play and the derived play-type possession records in the graph database, frozen as of 2026-06-19 with a recorded hash/date: 2022-23 to 2024-25 complete; 2025-26 regular season complete (2026-04-13); 2025-26 playoffs partial (excluded from primary; held out for confirmation after 2026-06-21). Record the labeling-fix version and the SF07 pipeline version used for comparison.

methodological_questions: Is the opponent's next-possession PPP after a given play type large enough to change AVOID labels?
Do own-team prior-possession lags predict outcomes beyond the current play type?
How do selection, outcome-derived labels, and mechanical floors (e.g., turnovers/makes leading to transition or inbound) confound next-possession effects?
What sample size and multiple-testing corrections are needed across play types?
args.query: next-possession opponent PPP after play type, AVOID label, lagged own-sequence effects, data quality of play-type labels

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

reasoning_details.text:
I'm checking whether the opponent's next-possession PPP after each play is large enough to justify AVOID labels, and whether own-sequence lags matter too. The SF07 aftershock shifts every play type by roughly the same +0.12–0.135, so that uniform change wouldn't separate one play type from another.

The baseline of 1.206 looks suspiciously high next to the own-next figure of 0.975, so it may be defined on a different set of transitions, possibly after a live turnover rather than a made shot. The aftershock was only measured after successes, which makes the made-basket versus miss split mechanical, and I should flag the labeling problems too: the OTHER foul bucket, DRIVE foul leakage, and initiation_type covering only 0.7%. I'm leaning toward proceeding with changes and deciding how to handle the partial 2025-26 playoffs, either by freezing the data version or holding that season back as a confirmatory sample.

I'm settling on the design now: estimating the opponent's next-possession scoring after each play relative to the play-type average, adjusted for the play's outcome, score, time, and lineup strength, and checking whether that gap would actually flip an AVOID label at a reasonable threshold. The own-sequence effect looks small, since it covers only about 4% of pairs, so it's mainly exploratory.

I'm working out how to test the falsification side: a lag-2 placebo, shuffled play-type labels within games, and a check on the opponent's previous possession before X to catch leakage. I'm also planning to compare against a generic dead-ball baseline, since whatever happens after X is mediated by how the possession ends.

I'm weighing whether the opponent's next-possession scoring after each play type is large enough to drive AVOID labels, and I need to condition on how X ends, since a made basket and a defensive rebound lead to very different next possessions. The uniform aftershock shift and the odd 1.206 baseline both suggest the comparison isn't matched, so I'm planning a decision rule, a multiplicity correction across the eight play types, and falsification checks like a lag-2 placebo and label shuffling.

I'm settling on rough weights for the outcomes: about 0.2 for the play-type-specific AVOID effect holding up, 0.3 for it being rejected, 0.25 for it being an artifact of a generic effect, 0.05 untestable, and 0.2 uncertain. I'd put the chance the question is testable at about 0.65, mainly held back by label error in the foul buckets and too little power for the own-sequence analysis.
